title: The U.S. has weapons in space
content: The U.S. has weapons in space | Scientific American New Issue: Orbital Catastrophe Ahead? Read Now September 15, 2026 3 min read Add Us On Google Add SciAm It’s official: The U.S. has weapons in space A high-ranking official announced yesterday that the U.S. military has deployed weapons into orbit to counter threats from Russia and China By Mary Randolph edited by Lee Billings Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink delivers a keynote address during the 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference at National Harbor, Md., on September 14, 2026. U.S. Air Force/Andy Morataya In a first for the U.S. Space Force since its inception six years ago, the military branch has announced the deployment of weapons in space. Speaking at the Air and Space Forces Association’s annual Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Monday, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink declared that the U.S. has placed offensive technology into orbit, though he did not disclose any details about the weapons. “We are increasing readiness against existing threats, and the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” he said. Although this is the first such acknowledgement from any global power, experts have long suspected space weapons are already a reality . In recent years, Russia has allegedly jammed communications satellites across Europe , and U.S. intelligence agencies have accused Russia of planning to put nuclear weapons in space . China, too, has demonstrated advanced capabilities for tracking and targeting satellites; these capabilities include a reusable space plane , similar to the U.S.’s X-37B, that could rendezvous with and capture adversarial spacecraft. Both Russia and China—as well as the U.S.—have a history of antisatellite missile tests and “cat and mouse” orbital encounters in which spacecraft maneuver to shadow or threaten others. The U.S. deployment is a matter of necessity, Meink said in a press conference on Monday. “Is there any question in the room, by anybody, about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons?” he said. “For over a decade, we’ve been talking about the fact, and we have expressed concern, that the Chinese and Russians were developing weapons for space. We need to focus on making sure we can protect ourselves operating in that environment.” According to Victoria Samson , chief director for space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation (SWF), the militarization is escalating rapidly in Earth orbit as more nations develop robust space programs. According to an SWF report co-authored by Samson from earlier this year, 13 countries have developed counterspace capabilities of some kind, including co-orbital satellites, which can disable or destroy other spacecraft, and space situational awareness satellites, which can track other objects in orbit. “A lot of countries are saying, ‘We depend upon very heavily our space capabilities for national security reasons. They’re at risk; it’s a threatening environment. Therefore we need to build offensive capabilities that can threaten others,’” Samson told Scientific American before the Space Force announcement. Despite their own well-documented military activity in space, both Russia and China responded to Monday’s announcement with statements warning against space militarization, with China opposing an “arms race” in the final frontier and Russia calling for the “complete demilitarization of space.” The current international framework for preventing space warfare is threadbare and filled with loopholes; signatories of the United Nations’ Outer Space Treaty of 1967 are merely obliged not to place weapons of mass destruction in orbit and to build no military bases and conduct no weapons testing on the moon or other planets. Regardless of who is most culpable in the ongoing push for more and better offensive off-world capabilities, experts fear this announcement will further escalate the situation, raising the chances of space warfare that could prove ruinous for the entire world. John Barentine , an astronomer and formerly a policy expert at the International Dark-Sky Association (now DarkSky International), believes the militarization of space will ultimately prove “unwinnable” and will require a stabilizing doctrine similar to the Cold War’s nuclear threat of mutually assured destruction . “I wonder if that’s not where we will end up with space militarization generally,” Barentine says, “where everybody rushes to acquire the technology, and we quickly realize that if war breaks out in space, it’s probably ‘game over’ for everybody.” Other experts aren’t necessarily convinced this announcement will change much inhe ta galactic game of chicken. Among them is Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “With this disclosure, the U.S. is hoping that the knowledge of weapons on orbit may change behaviors. But without knowing exactly what these weapons could do and having a general sense of when the U.S. would decide to use them, it is hard to see China or Russia significantly altering their behaviors,” Swope says. “Deterrence requires convincing an adversary you will use a weapon, not just that you have one.” Subscribe to Support Independent Journalism Great science journalism requires human expertise, time, effort and creativity.
